newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: INTERVIEW - Holderbank says Europe weighs on shares.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Holderbank says Europe weighs on shares.

text.p: Investors are giving too much weight to western Europe's stagnant construction sector in valuing shares in Holderbank Financiere Glarus AG, the world's leading cement maker, the company's chairman said.

Chairman and managing director Thomas Schmidheiny told Reuters he believed Holderbank's established or growing positions in thriving world markets and new modern facilities starting up this year were underweighted in the share price.

But Schmidheiny said he saw no reason why the bearer share should not reach 1,300 Swiss francs by the end of the year after recent gains based on well-received 1996 operating results and steps to cut west European capacity.
"The actual stagnation of (western) Europe is in my opinion too heavyweighted in the stock price," Schmidheiny told Reuters in a recent interview.

Schmidheiny said western Europe, despite poor cement demand, would remain a profitable cash generator due to a restructuring plan announced last month that included shutting one cement plant in Switzerland.
"We have stated very clearly that we are convinced that cash-generation and profits in Europe will be stable," Schmidheiny said.
Holderbank last month said 1996 net profit after minorities rose 9.6 percent to 493 million Swiss francs, more than expected by analysts.
But it also took a one-time charge of 607 million Swiss francs ($422 million) for trimming capacity in sated markets in western Europe, slashing net profit to 43 million.
Holderbank's bearer shares hovered last year between 900 and 1,000 Swiss francs before rising above 1,000 in early January. It broke 1,200 last week and closed on Monday up eight francs at 1,240.
Asked whether the share could be worth 1,300 by year's end, as some analysts forecast, Schmidheiny said:
"I would guess the stock market will perform generally quite well this year and with the potential we have built in, I don't see any reason why the share price should not (hit 1,300)."
Schmidheiny said Holderbank would benefit from strong growth in North and Latin America and eastern Europe, where it is well-positioned, as well as Asia-Pacific, where it is building a presence.
"I am quite confident that Latin America and (North) America will go on for another 18 months in the mood in which it is in today, so that gives us quite a strong bottom line position," he said.
Schmidheiny said these factors were not yet weighted strongly enough in the share price.
"The other thing which is not reflected very strongly is that by the end of 1997 we will have completely new kiln equipment for about six million tonnes (of cement)," he said.
Holderbank, which has capacity for 77 million tonnes, is bringing new high-tech plants on line in Lebanon, Germany, Australia, Columbia and the United States.
Another facility will follow when Holderbank starts up its first cement plant in Vietnam by around mid-1998.

Of Holderbank's 1996 operating profit of 1.1 billion Swiss francs, the largest contribution came from Latin America with 291 million, followed by Europe excluding Switzerland (271 million), North America (262 million), Africa-Asia-Oceania (188 million) and Switzerland (91 million).
